title: FLUCS: a modular GPU-native framework for fluid and plasma turbulence
summary: We present FLUCS, an open-source framework for solving systems of partial differential equations efficiently on graphics processing units (GPUs), targeting models of fluid and plasma turbulence. It comprises a set of numerical solvers specialised for a well-defined class of problems and independently developed systems that supply specific systems of equations. This allows different models to share numerical infrastructure while retaining control over their individual implementation and optimisation. The present release provides a Fourier pseudospectral solver for one-, two-, and three-dimensional periodic domains solved on a single NVIDIA GPU, with integrating-factor time integration and several time-stepping and dealiasing methods. We verify its convergence, quantify its computational costs, and demonstrate its application to three reduced models of fusion and astrophysical plasma turbulence.

title: Stress-enhanced diffusion in Yukawa crystals
summary: Self-diffusion in crystallized Coulomb (Yukawa) plasmas proceeds by the thermally activated formation of vacancy-interstitial pairs and the migration of these defects through the lattice, commonly known as Frenkel pairs in the materials literature. Molecular dynamics has recently resolved an Eyring law for diffusion in unstrained crystals, which we generalize to deformed crystals in this work. We simulate sheared Yukawa crystals and show that a static elastic strain exponentially enhances diffusion due to the additional elastic energy stored in the region that participates in Frenkel pair formation relative to the unstrained crystal: $D(\varepsilon)=D_0(Γ^{*})\exp[V^{*}σ/k_{\rm B}T]$, with $σ=\tfrac12μ\varepsilon^{2}$ the elastic energy density stored by the shear strain $\varepsilon$ and $V^{*}$ the activation volume. We find a single activation volume $N_{\rm act} = n_iV^{*}\simeq31$ suffices for typical astrophysical screenings with a reduction at higher screening. This suggests Frenkel pair formation requires only a brief coordination of the nearest neighbors at a thermal maximum in oscillation. Stress-enhanced diffusion supplies a microphysical mechanism for creep in strained neutron star crusts and crystallizing white dwarf cores.

title: Equipartition between Alfvénic turbulence and energetic ions as the origin of the -5 common spectrum in the heliosphere
summary: Suprathermal ion tails throughout the heliosphere follow a ``common spectrum,'' $f(v)\propto v^{-5}$. We show that scale-by-scale equipartition between strong Alfvénic turbulence and the ions it accelerates predicts both this exponent and the absolute amplitude, $F(v)=B^2/(16π^3 m_i v^5)$, with no free parameters. The prediction agrees within a factor of a few with ACE and Voyager 1 spectra across three decades in magnetic energy. We argue that this saturated level is reached where strong turbulence accelerates particles locally; quiet-time tails lie well below it, consistent with nonlocal acceleration.

title: Teacher-guided multi-task learning for integrated plasma monitoring on EAST
summary: This paper integrates tokamak plasma disruption prediction, Edge-Localized Mode (ELM) monitoring, Multifaceted Asymmetric Radiation From the Edge (MARFE) detection, and H/L-mode identification into a unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL) model. This integration aims to realize MTL's potential for improving task performance while reducing inference time. However, on datasets constructed from selected EAST discharges recorded between 2015 and 2020, this study found that the traditional MTL method underperformed the corresponding Single-Task Learning (STL) method on some tasks. This performance degradation is the well-known issue of negative transfer. To address this issue, this study proposes the teacher-guided MTL method, using task-specific STL ensembles (teachers) to guide the training of an MTL model (student). The ensemble teachers guide training through soft-target distillation losses for each task of the MTL student model, and increased weighting of each shot's peak-disruptivity window in the disruption prediction label-supervised loss. Test-set results showed that the teacher-guided MTL method outperformed the corresponding STL method in ROC-AUC for all four tasks, eliminating the negative transfer observed with the traditional MTL method. In addition, on the same single GPU or single physical CPU core, the MTL student model can substantially reduce the inference time required to generate all four task outputs compared with the four STL baseline models. This paper offers a promising route to plasma monitoring systems that cover a broader range of phenomena, improve per-task performance and reduce inference time with limited real-time computational resources, supporting future high-performance plasma operation.

title: Plasmoid Instability in Inhomogeneous Current Sheets
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, submitted to Plasma and Fusion Research
summary: Plasmoid instability in inhomogeneous current sheets is investigated using electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulations of collisionless magnetic reconnection. Simulations with and without small random perturbations are compared to examine the effects of symmetry breaking and spatial inhomogeneity. The current-sheet width immediately before disruption remains close to the electron skin depth, whereas the disruption aspect ratio varies significantly between primary and later current sheets. Random perturbations also produce asymmetric plasmoid topologies in which neighboring X points no longer share a common separatrix. These results suggest that spatial inhomogeneity is an important factor in the disruption of dynamically evolving current sheets.

title: Accelerating Computation and Resolving Extraneous Roots in the Kinetic Plasma Dispersion Relation Solver BO
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Code available at https://github.com/FusionAlpha/botian
summary: Kinetic dispersion relations are widely used to study waves and instabilities in space, astrophysical, and laboratory plasmas. Iterative root searches depend on initial guesses and may fail to converge or miss important branches. The BO/PDRK solvers [Comput. Phys. Commun. 244, 343-371 (2019)] use rational pole expansions to transform the nonlinear dispersion relation into a matrix eigenvalue problem, obtaining all roots of the approximated relation in one calculation. However, high cyclotron harmonics enlarge the matrix and slow computation, while extraneous roots are difficult to separate from physical modes. We develop BO-T (BO-Tian), an improved version of BO combining two methods. First, for matrix reduction, BO-T applies rank factorization to combined residue matrices, preserving the rational dispersion relation and accounting for the removed pole eigenvalues. Second, for root screening, BO-T uses contour comparison between approximate and reference kinetic dispersion matrices along a closed contour enclosing no poles. This provides a sufficient condition for preserving local root counts, with error bounds for isolated roots and criteria for growth rate signs. Benchmarks on representative electrostatic and electromagnetic cases show speedups of about 10 to 140 for matrix assembly and eigenvalue calculation, exceeding 30 in most cases with high cyclotron harmonics. Root screening recovers the main unstable branches in agreement with published and archived dispersion curves.

title: An approximate separation of the electron and positron degrees of freedom in the Dirac-Heisenberg-Wigner formalism
summary: Here we study the quantum relativistic phase-space description of the Dirac field referred to as the Dirac--Heisenberg--Wigner (DHW) formalism. By applying a systematic expansion procedure in weak electromagnetic fields (compared to the Schwinger critical field) and slow temporal and long spatial scales (compared to the Compton scales), the 16 scalar phase-space functions of the DHW equations can be reduced to 8 scalars. By making a further change of variables, the equations can be interpreted as four evolution equations for the electron degrees of freedom and four for the positron degrees of freedom. We refer to these equations as the weakly coupled electron-positron (WCEP) limit of the DHW equations. Unlike the case after a Foldy--Wouthuysen transformation has been made, the electron and positron degrees of freedom remain weakly coupled. Naturally, further approximations can be made on the 4+4 equations so that only 4 equations for one particle species remain. Importantly, the expansion scheme can be carried out to all orders, in which case the reduced 4+4 model, contrary to other reduced models, will cover most quantum relativistic effects. Specifically, this includes vacuum polarization, a phenomenon that otherwise has been added phenomenologically, but here appears naturally as a feature of the general expansion scheme.

title: Stabilization of counter propagating currents by energy conservation in collisions
summary: Current filamentation generates magnetic fields and shapes electron transport in dense plasmas, where collisions can either suppress or enhance its growth. Here we show that conserving electron kinetic energy in a collisional model can change both the dominant instability and its characteristic wavelength. We develop a linear kinetic theory for drifting, anisotropic electron populations with a relaxation operator that conserves particle number and laboratory-frame kinetic energy while allowing momentum transfer to a stationary ion background. For counterstreaming currents, energy conservation maintains the stabilizing influence of charge separation over a broader range of collision frequencies than a model conserving particle number alone. At intermediate collision rates, the resulting suppression of transverse filamentation allows a nearly aperiodic oblique mode to dominate, reducing the maximum growth rate and shifting the wavelength of the fastest-growing perturbation. Two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations support predicted growth rates of up to more than a magnitude lower than expected without energy conserving collision.

title: Machine learning surrogates for multi-geometry EDGE2D-EIRENE studies of MAST Upgrade
comment: Abstract shortened for arXiv; see manuscript for full abstract
summary: Two-dimensional edge plasma transport simulations provide a detailed description of divertor plasma behaviour, but their computational cost limits large parameter scans and iterative modelling. We present a database of 23,379 converged EDGE2D-EIRENE simulations for MAST Upgrade (MAST-U), spanning three divertor magnetic configurations, variations in separatrix density and input power, deuterium fuelling locations, and nitrogen seeding rates and locations. Independent multilayer perceptron surrogates are trained for twelve scalar outputs, including divertor front positions, target electron temperature and core-edge boundary quantities. On a held-out test set, the surrogates achieve $0.9462 \leq R^2 \leq 0.9994$, substantially outperforming linear regression baselines. Dense surrogate scans quantify the dependence of carbon radiation front motion on separatrix density, divertor geometry and fuelling location. Nitrogen seeding scans reveal a strong dependence on seeding location, with high-field-side seeding rapidly reducing core-boundary electron temperature, while divertor seeding produces little response. Batch inference for all twelve outputs at 786,432 operating points takes 1.76 s on GPU, compared with a median wall time of 2.61 hours using four CPU cores for separate EDGE2D-EIRENE simulations. These models enable rapid comparison of geometry and source-location effects on divertor and core-boundary conditions within the sampled simulation domain.
